Requesting after=Y filters updatedAt < Y.updatedAt (Jan 2), which excludes X (updatedAt Jan 10), so X is skipped. Requesting after=X (updatedAt Jan 10) returns Z and Y again. B's own test passes only because it pins updatedAt and not createdAt, and A's test doesn't use the cursor.

The cursor's sort key and filter key no longer match. Concrete scenario: articles X (created Jan 1) and Y (created Jan 2), then X is edited so its updatedAt is Jan 5. List order is Y, X. A request with ?limit=1&after=y filters updatedAt < Y.updatedAt (Jan 2), which excludes X (updatedAt Jan 5), so the next page is empty and X is skipped. Conversely, articles can be repeated or skipped whenever updatedAt order differs from createdAt order. B's own test passes only because it pins updatedAt while createdAt stays in insertion order matching it.

Neither breaks the other's assumptions; B's read-side normalization is actually only fully correct with A's write-side normalization. They don't duplicate work, since one handles storing and the other handles querying. Legacy mixed-case tags in the DB would not be matched, but that is a pre-existing data concern, not a merge conflict.

For example: create an article with a unique tag, GET /api/tags (cached), delete the article (tag removed from DB), GET /api/tags still lists the tag. A's test only queries prisma directly, so it passes; B's cache assumption that creation is the only tag-mutating event is broken by A's new tag deletion.

The stored value becomes bcrypt(bcrypt(newPassword)), so after POST /api/user/password the user can no longer log in with the new password (login compares the plain password against the double hash). B's own test only checks the stored value differs from plain text, so it still passes. This is a concrete runtime breakage that neither change causes alone. It is also an intent overlap, since both changes independently add password hashing at different layers.

rows.label: conflict

B adds a views counter, incremented via prisma.article.update on every article GET. With @updatedAt in the merged schema, the views increment also bumps updatedAt on every read, so updatedAt (which A intends to mean last content modification) changes on each view. Articles would show as 'updated' whenever they are merely read, and any ordering or display by updatedAt becomes wrong. Neither change causes this alone: before A, B's update didn't touch updatedAt; after A alone, only real edits bump it.

A deletes orphaned tags from the database at article-deletion time. B filters the tag listing to tags attached to at least one article. They are individually correct and compatible at runtime. But in the merged code the system both cleans orphans on delete and filters them on read, which is redundant. Their tests even assert identical behavior. One of the two mechanisms should be removed.

The second filter is redundant. Both changes also rewrite the same existing test in articles.int.test.ts identically and each add a separate new integration test for the same behavior. One of the two fixes (and one of the new tests) should be removed.

B adds a requireArticleAuthor middleware to the delete route. Merged, a non-author request is rejected twice, with the same 403 and the same logic, and the controller repeats the user and article lookups the middleware already did. The behavior is correct, but the ownership check is duplicated and one of the two should be removed. Both changes also delete the same 'known bug' test and add near-identical new tests.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A truncates generated slugs to 100 characters, while Change B rejects titles longer than 150 characters in the create validator. Both address overly long titles but at different layers (slug length vs. title length) and with different limits. They are complementary rather than duplicative: titles up to 150 chars are accepted and slugs are truncated to 100. A possible concern is two distinct long titles sharing the same first 100 chars producing identical slugs, but that collision risk is inherent to A's truncation and unrelated to B's validator; if the slug has a unique constraint, handling would be in existing code. B's integration test uses 'x'.repeat(150) which slugs to 100 x's, still valid and unique for that user. No concrete scenario where merged code breaks or duplicates work.

rows.explanation: Change A adds database indexes on Article.authorUsername and Article.updatedAt, a pure performance optimization. Change B adds a sort query parameter that orders the article list by createdAt or updatedAt (default updatedAt desc). They are compatible: the updatedAt index supports the default sort, and neither change breaks assumptions of the other. The author index helps the author filter. Sorting by createdAt has no index, but that is only a performance gap, not incorrect behavior or duplicated work.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: A caches the tags list and invalidates it via a prisma middleware on writes to Tag or Article. B's change deletes orphan tags after an article delete with prisma.tag.deleteMany. Since B's code calls prisma.article.delete first (model Article, action delete, invalidates cache) and then prisma.tag.deleteMany (model Tag, action deleteMany, also in WRITE_ACTIONS), the cache is invalidated after the orphan cleanup too. The middleware awaits next() before clearing, so the cache is cleared after the delete completes. There is a minor race (a concurrent getTags between the article delete and tag cleanup could cache stale tags, but the subsequent deleteMany clears the cache again). No scenario where merged code serves stale orphan tags beyond what the invalidation covers. The two changes solve different problems and stay correct together.

rows.label: no_conflict

B adds a separate POST /api/user/password endpoint that requires the current password and hashes the new one before storing it. They do not break each other at runtime: B hashes before calling userSetPasswordPrisma, which bypasses userUpdatePrisma, so there is no double hashing. A's PUT path hashes once. There is a mild intent overlap, since two routes can now change a password. But B's endpoint adds distinct behavior (verifying the current password), and A's fix is still needed because PUT /api/user would otherwise store plain text. Both changes are correct together.

B's tests use RESET_TOKEN_SECRET, which is present, and no B code reads JWT_SECRET. The two changes do not interact at runtime and do not solve the same problem.

In the merged code, a plain GET /api/articles uses the default of 10, while GET /api/articles?page=1 returns 20 and ?page=2 starts at offset 20. So the plain default page holds 10 articles while numbered pages hold 20, and paging with page=1 then page=2 is inconsistent with the default listing. Neither test breaks alone, since they hit different code paths, but the two page-size definitions contradict each other (10 vs 20).

Change A normalizes the email in the controllers via a new normalizeEmail util; Change B normalizes it in the DB helpers (userCreatePrisma and userGetEmailPrisma) with inline trim().toLowerCase(). Merged, the email is normalized twice on every register and login path. The result is idempotent and behaves correctly, but the work is duplicated and there are two competing normalization mechanisms (the util and the inline logic), plus two overlapping integration tests. One of the two approaches should be removed.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes article updates re-derive the slug from the new title, so the article's slug (its primary key) can now change. Change B introduces a RecentView table keyed by (username, slug) that stores the slug as a plain string with no foreign key to Article and no cascade on rename. Merged, a user who viewed 'old-title' has a RecentView row with slug 'old-title'; after the author renames the article to 'new-title', that row dangles. recentArticlesPrisma then looks up 'old-title', finds no article, and silently drops it via flatMap. The renamed article disappears from the user's recent list until they view it again under the new slug, and if they view it again they get a duplicate stale row that eats into the KEEP=10 window. Before A, slugs never changed on update so B's slug-keyed design was safe. A's tests do not cover this interaction, and B's design silently assumes slugs are stable.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A switches list ordering from updatedAt to createdAt. Change B adds an ?after=<slug> cursor that filters with updatedAt < cursor.updatedAt, assuming the list is ordered by updatedAt desc. Concrete scenario: articles X (created Jan 1, edited Jan 10) and Y (created Jan 2, updated Jan 2). The list orders Y, X by createdAt. Calling ?after=Y filters updatedAt < Jan 2, which excludes X (updatedAt Jan 10), so X is skipped. Calling ?after=X returns Y again, because Y.updatedAt < Jan 10, and Y was already shown before X. Pagination via cursor therefore skips or duplicates items. B's own test passes only because createdAt order and updatedAt order coincide in its setup.

The two changes do not solve the same problem, but the new endpoint silently violates the invariant A establishes about what user images may be.
